clinicalPearls: Large unilateral hyperpigmented patch, most often over the shoulder, upper back or chest, that typically becomes more apparent around puberty in adolescent males
Progressive coarse hypertrichosis commonly develops within the patch, usually after the pigmentation has appeared
Androgen sensitivity is implicated, explaining the male predominance, pubertal onset and terminal hair growth
An underlying smooth-muscle hamartoma may cause slight induration or perifollicular papules within the lesion
Becker naevus syndrome describes association with ipsilateral hypoplasia of the breast or nipple and skeletal or soft-tissue anomalies
There is increased epidermal melanisation without proliferation of naevus cells, and malignant transformation is not a recognised feature
Management is largely reassurance; laser can address pigmentation and hair, though results are variable and recurrence is common
reference.pathophysiology: Becker naevus is regarded as a mosaic organoid hamartoma showing increased epidermal melanisation and melanocyte activity, epidermal acanthosis and hyperplasia of arrector pili smooth muscle, rather than a proliferation of naevus cells. Local upregulation of androgen receptors is thought to underlie its typical onset at puberty, its predilection for males and the development of terminal hair. The associated smooth-muscle hamartoma explains the occasional induration and follicular prominence.
additionalInvestigations: Clinical examination and dermoscopy of the pigmented patch
Assessment for hypertrichosis and follicular papules within the lesion
Examination for ipsilateral breast, nipple or skeletal anomalies suggesting Becker naevus syndrome
Skin biopsy where the diagnosis is uncertain, showing epidermal and smooth-muscle changes
redFlags: Associated breast/nipple hypoplasia or skeletal anomaly indicating Becker naevus syndrome
Atypical change, nodularity or rapid growth prompting exclusion of another lesion
Marked induration suggesting a prominent smooth-muscle hamartoma component
reference.prognosis: The naevus is benign and stable, persisting lifelong with permanent pigmentation and hypertrichosis; it carries no meaningful malignant potential, and treatment is undertaken only for cosmetic reasons.
pitfalls: Confusing it with a congenital melanocytic naevus or a large café-au-lait macule
Overlooking Becker naevus syndrome when there are associated anomalies
Over-treating a benign lesion, with variable and often incomplete laser results
Attributing the hypertrichosis to an endocrine disorder rather than the naevus itself
management: Reassure that the naevus is benign with negligible malignant potential and that treatment is undertaken for cosmetic reasons only
Offer camouflage cosmetics as a simple non-invasive option for the pigmentation
Provide laser hair removal for troublesome hypertrichosis within the lesion
Consider pigment-directed laser therapy for the hyperpigmentation, accepting a variable and often incomplete response
Examine for ipsilateral breast, nipple or skeletal anomalies that would indicate Becker naevus syndrome
Document stability with serial photography rather than routine biopsy
